knowledge_point.title: Finding the Rank or Nullity of a Matrix Given a Description of the Column or Null Space

question.:question/problem: Find $\text{rank}(A)$ given that $\text{Null}(A)=\{\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}\,|\,\,{x}_{2},{x}_{3}\in R\}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
According to the rank-nullity theorem, if $A$ is a matrix with $n$ columns, then 

$$
\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A)=n.
$$

For the given matrix, we have $n=4,$ since this is the number of components in each of the vectors of the null space. 

Also, since 

$$
\text{Null}(A)=\{{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\,|\,\,{x}_{2},{x}_{3}\in R\}
$$

we conclude that $\text{nullity}(A)=2.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A) & =n \\ \text{rank}(A)+2 & =4 \\ \text{rank}(A) & =4-2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

According to the rank-nullity theorem, if $A$ is a matrix with $n$ columns, then 

$$
\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A)=n.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A) & =n \\ 1+\text{nullity}(A) & =5 \\ \text{nullity}(A) & =5-1 \\ \text{dim(Null}(A)) & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Find $\text{rank}(A)$ given that

$$
\text{Null}(A)=\{\begin{bmatrix}-{x}_{3} \\ 3{x}_{3} \\ -3{x}_{2} \\ 3{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}\,|\,\,{x}_{2},{x}_{3}\in R\}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
According to the rank-nullity theorem, if $A$ is a matrix with $n$ columns, then 

$$
\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A)=n.
$$

For the given matrix, we have $n=4,$ since this is the number of components in each of the vectors of the null space. 

Also, since 

$$
\text{Null}(A)=\{{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ -3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\,|\,\,{x}_{2},{x}_{3}\in R\}
$$

we conclude that $\text{nullity}(A)=2.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A) & =n \\ \text{rank}(A)+2 & =4 \\ \text{rank}(A) & =4-2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$
